## TL;DR
`repoos restart` restarts this repo's server whether it is a RepoOS managed service, an external launchd/systemd supervisor (including system-domain LaunchDaemons — the Kamrai case), or a hand-run `repoos serve`. This round clears the pass-4 review: the restart now names every kind of in-flight work it interrupts (not just engineers), the managed-service path can no longer bounce a service that is not the located server, and the supervisor detector refuses rather than guessing when it cannot rule out supervision.

## Work and rationale
Pass 4 left five findings. All are addressed:

1. **The stop warning only covered engineers.** A real SIGTERM shutdown runs `reviews.cancelAll()`, `freeformRuns.cancelAll()`, `previews.stopAll()` and `devTargets.stopAll()`, but `cmdRestart` warned only about `activeEngineers`. I added `activeReviews`, `activeFreeformRuns`, `activeDevTargets` and `activePreviews` to `/api/health` (using existing manager accessors plus two new `activeCount()` methods on `FreeformRunManager` and `DevTargetManager`), a `fetchCancelledWork` probe in `server-restart.ts`, and a `cancelled: CancelledWork` payload on `onBeforeStop`. The CLI now prints exactly what a stop kills (reviews, previews) versus what it briefly interrupts and re-adopts (engineers, PM runs, dev targets), and says plainly when nothing is in flight. This keeps the #0214 promise — engineering/PM children are durable and re-adopted — while no longer hiding the reviews and previews that a real shutdown does kill and must re-spawn.
2. **The managed path could restart the wrong server.** `classifyRestartPath` checked `getServiceStatus(root).status === "running"` without comparing the located server's port. With a managed service on 7272 and a hand-run server on 7373, `repoos restart --port 7373` would bounce the service and then time out. The guard is now `managed.port === server.port`; `getServiceStatus(root)` defaults to this repo's managed port, so a match always means the service owns the located listener.
3. **Failure after SIGTERM left the user guessing.** The external-supervisor timeout now always prints a usable command — the supervisor's own restart when known, otherwise a `repoos serve` start — instead of an undefined `manualCommand`. The hand-run failure paths replay the resolved serve flags (not the possibly-empty stored ones) in the manual command.
4. **The refusal manual command did not restart.** The `uncertain` branch printed a bare `kill <pid>`, which only stops the server. It now prints a stop-then-start sequence and explains that killing lets a supervisor respawn it, so the command shown actually restores service either way.
5. **Test gaps.** Added a test that the cancelled-work summary reaches the result, a supervisor-detect test that an unreadable parent is `uncertain` (not hand-run), and systemd tests against captured `systemctl status <pid>` shapes (system unit vs. user unit vs. the rejected `user@<uid>.service`).

I also tightened `detectDarwinSupervisor`: when `launchctl list` (and the domain prints) produce no row AND `ps` cannot read the parent, the result is now `uncertain`. `launchctl print pid/N` exits 0 for a nonexistent pid, so a parse miss proved nothing; refusing is the conservative choice that keeps a supervised server from being SIGTERM'd into a race with its own respawn.

## Approaches tried
I considered routing `repoos restart` through the in-process reload handover (`POST /api/server/restart`) so in-flight reviews and previews survive. I rejected it: the reload is a server-owned, in-process API. `repoos restart` exists precisely for the cases the API cannot reach — a server that is stale, wedged, or started by a supervisor RepoOS does not manage. A restart the user asks for by running a CLI is a different operation from a build-staleness reload, so the honest design is an accurate warning plus a correct classification, which is what this round delivers.

For supervisor detection I reused the `pid<TAB>status<TAB>label` row parser for `launchctl print system`/`gui/<uid>` (same columns as `launchctl list`), so no second parser was needed. Reading a plist for the label was rejected: a label alone does not map to the running pid.

## Challenges and blockers
No real non-sudo `KeepAlive` LaunchDaemon was available to respawn-test live, and I cannot verify a system-domain `kickstart` without root. Detection is covered by captured-output fixtures only; the live respawn timing is unverified here. This is the same limitation every pass has flagged, and it needs the reporter's mini to close out fully.

## Key learnings
- A stop is not a reload. Anywhere the code says "restart" and means SIGTERM, the distinct set of killed-vs-adopted work has to be named, or the warning is wrong in one direction or the other.
- Detection code must fail closed. `launchctl print` answering successfully for a nonexistent pid is exactly the kind of "succeeds but proves nothing" signal that turns a conservative classifier into a dangerous one; refuse when no positive mapping was found.
- When two servers of different kinds can share a repo, "is there a managed service?" is the wrong question — "is the located listener the managed one?" is.
